nameStory: The marsh pink gets its name from its lovely pink star-shaped flowers and its love of salty marshlands. It's also called "rose of Plymouth," a romantic name that honors both its rosy blooms and the coastal Massachusetts region where early botanists first studied it extensively.
description: Marsh pink is a delicate annual wildflower that brings splashes of bright pink to New England's coastal salt marshes. This charming plant grows 6 to 18 inches tall with slender stems that branch near the top. Its most striking feature is its star-shaped flowers with five pointed pink petals that seem to glow against the marsh grasses. The whole plant has a neat, upright appearance despite growing in the challenging conditions of salty wetlands.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink five-petaled flowers shaped like perfect stars, each about an inch across with a bright yellow center and delicate white lines radiating from the middle

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, feeling smooth and slightly succulent to help the plant cope with salty conditions

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright stems that branch into a loose cluster near the top, giving the whole plant an elegant candelabra-like shape

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small oval capsules that split open when ripe to release tiny brown seeds that feel like fine sand between your fingers

habitat: Marsh pink thrives in the challenging environment of coastal salt marshes, particularly along the edges where saltwater regularly floods the area. You'll find it growing in sandy or muddy soils that can handle both salt spray and periodic submersion in brackish water. It's most common along the Massachusetts coast and is quite rare elsewhere in New England.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of narrow leaves, barely noticeable among the marsh grasses.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through September, when the spectacular pink star flowers open in the morning sun and attract butterflies and bees.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, eventually splitting open to scatter seeds across the marsh on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving no trace above ground until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Marsh pink is one of the few wildflowers that can actually survive being completely submerged in saltwater during high tides, then emerge hours later looking perfectly fresh and ready to bloom again!
confusionNotes: The star-shaped pink flowers make marsh pink quite distinctive in its salt marsh habitat, where few other pink wildflowers can survive the salty conditions. The combination of the coastal wetland location and the perfect five-pointed star flowers sets it apart from any inland pink wildflowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name "rose of Plymouth," this plant isn't actually related to roses at all—it belongs to the gentian family. The "rose" in the name simply refers to its pink color, while "Plymouth" reflects where it was extensively studied by early New England botanists.
compareHints: Marsh pink differs from its cousin Plymouth gentian by having consistently pink flowers (Plymouth gentian is usually white or pale pink) and growing in salt marshes rather than sandy shores. Unlike the rosepink, which grows inland and has square stems, marsh pink has round stems and requires the salty coastal environment. The slender rose gentian is much taller and has narrower petals than marsh pink's broad, star-shaped blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Plymouth rose gentian is distinguished from marsh pink by having exactly five petals instead of 8-12, and from other rose gentians by its coastal pond habitat and the specific white star pattern radiating from its yellow center.
Slender rose gentian is much more delicate and narrow-stemmed than its relatives like marsh pink, which tends to be more robust.
Among its rose gentian relatives, rosepink is distinguished by its square stem - Plymouth gentian and marsh pink both have round stems.
